extraction.name: HELVIPAD
extraction.description: A real-world dataset for omnidirectional stereo depth estimation, consisting of 39,553 paired top-bottom 360° images with corresponding depth and disparity maps, captured from a robot navigating in dynamic human environments including crowded indoor and outdoor scenes with various lighting conditions.
extraction.creator: Mehdi Zayene, Jannik Endres, Albias Havolli, Charles Corbière, Salim Cherkaoui, Alexandre Kontouli, Alexandre Alahi
extraction.citeAs: @article{zayene2024helvipad, title={HELVIPAD: A Real-World Dataset for Omnidirectional Stereo Depth Estimation}, author={Zayene, Mehdi and Endres, Jannik and Havolli, Albias and Corbi\`ere, Charles and Cherkaoui, Salim and Kontouli, Alexandre and Alahi, Alexandre}, journal={arXiv preprint arXiv:2411.18335}, year={2024}}
extraction.rai:dataCollection: Data were collected using a custom-built rig equipped with two Ricoh Theta V 360° cameras in a vertical top-bottom arrangement with a 19.1 cm baseline, capturing equirectangular images at 30 fps, paired with an Ouster OS1-64 LiDAR sensor operating at 10 fps, mounted 45.0 cm below the bottom camera. A central processor manages data capture and ensures device synchronization. The rig was mounted on a custom-built, remotely controlled robot chassis for mobility.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionMissingData: Given the sparse nature of LiDAR point clouds compared to high-resolution camera images, ground-truth depth labels cover only a fraction of the total pixels.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: Raw data consists of equirectangular images from two Ricoh Theta V 360° cameras and 3D point clouds from an Ouster OS1-64 LiDAR sensor, collected across a university campus in indoor and outdoor environments.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: LiDAR point clouds are projected onto equirectangular images through coordinate transformation and optimization. Initial rotation and translation transformations align the camera lens as the coordinate system's center. Transformed points are converted to spherical coordinates and projected onto the equirectangular plane. Rotation and translation parameters are optimized by minimizing error between projected points and their corresponding image locations.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Images and depth maps are cropped to remove unnecessary regions (sky, ground) and downsized from 1024 pixels width to 512 pixels. Depth values are converted to disparity values via spherical disparity equation. A depth completion pipeline is applied to increase label density through temporal aggregation of point clouds, interpolation on spherical grid points, and filtering based on uncertainty and out-of-distribution thresholds.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Depth and disparity labels are generated by projecting LiDAR 3D point clouds onto equirectangular images. An augmented training set with increased label density is created using a depth completion pipeline that aggregates temporal point clouds, interpolates depth values, and filters uncertain points.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: To assess alignment accuracy between LiDAR projections and images, pixel error was calculated by measuring Euclidean distances between 200 randomly selected LiDAR points and their image positions, resulting in an average error of 1.7 pixels. When selecting points from visually challenging areas (e.g., object edges), the error remains relatively low at 8.0 pixels.
extraction.rai:machineAnnotationTools: LiDAR sensor (Ouster OS1-64) for depth measurement, custom depth completion pipeline for label augmentation
extraction.rai:personalSensitiveInformation: The dataset captures human pedestrians in dynamic environments, including crowded indoor and outdoor scenes.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: Indoor-trained models show clear limitation in generalizing to outdoor scenes, particularly at night. The dataset exhibits an exponential decay in pixel percentage with increasing depth, correlating with the decrease in LiDAR precision over longer distances. A distinct concentration of short-range distances within the 0–10 meter range is attributed to the LiDAR laser capturing the ground surface in each environment.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: The depth completion approach is limited for fast-moving objects like cars due to the temporal aggregation window. Occlusions were not explicitly handled, though the small LiDAR-camera baseline minimizes their impact. The dataset is collected on a university campus, which may limit generalization to other environments. Ground-truth depth labels cover only a fraction of total pixels due to sparse LiDAR point clouds. The depth completion method does not provide labels for pixels at object boundaries.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: The dataset is designed for training, validation, and testing of omnidirectional stereo depth estimation models. It serves as a foundational resource for developing and benchmarking models capable of navigating in human environments. The train-val set includes 20 sequences with 29,407 frames, and the test split consists of 6 sequences with 10,146 frames.

name.evidence: We introduce HELVIPAD, a real-world dataset for omnidirectional stereo depth estimation, featuring 40K video frames from video sequences across diverse environments

description.evidence: We introduce HELVIPAD, a real-world dataset for omnidirectional stereo depth estimation, featuring 40K video frames from video sequences across diverse environments, including crowded indoor and outdoor scenes with various lighting conditions. Collected using two 360° cameras in a top-bottom setup and a LiDAR sensor, the dataset includes accurate depth and disparity labels by projecting 3D point clouds onto equirectangular images.

rai:dataCollection.evidence: To assemble a dataset capturing human pedestrian activity, we built a custom rig and collected data across distinct scenes, encompassing indoor (e.g., corridors, halls) and outdoor (e.g., squares, external parking, footpaths) settings in various lighting conditions on a university campus. The rig features two Ricoh Theta V 360° cameras in a top-bottom setup with a 19.1 cm baseline, capturing equirectangular images at 30 fps, paired with a Ouster OS1-64 LiDAR sensor with a vertical field of view of 42.4°, operating at 10 fps, and mounted 45.0 cm below the bottom camera.

A central processor manages data capture and ensures device synchronization.

rai:dataCollectionTimeframe.evidence: The HELVIPAD dataset includes 26 video sequences captured between December 2023 and February 2024

rai:dataManipulationProtocol.evidence: At the beginning of each recorded session, we select a set of key 3D points in the point cloud obtained by the LiDAR scans on a 19x19 chessboard, focusing on corners and edge midpoints to obtain their coordinates. The corresponding image pixel positions are selected in the equirectangular bottom image. We apply initial rotation and translation transformations Rinit, Tinit to make the camera lens the coordinate system's center, ensuring alignment with the camera's viewpoint: pcam i=RinitpLiDAR,i+Tinit. The transformed points are then converted into spherical coordinates (r, θ, ϕ) to match the structure of equirectangular images, and projected onto the equirectangular plane. The core step of the mapping process is the optimization of the rotation and translation parameters, achieved by minimizing the error between the projected points and their corresponding location on the equirectangular images.

rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol.evidence: After cropping unnecessary regions (sky, ground), the resulting dataset comprises 39,553 paired images with their corresponding depth and disparity maps, at a resolution of 1920×512 pixels. To address this issue, we develop a fully automated depth completion pipeline tailored for 360° images. Existing depth completion methods share the idea of aggregating point clouds but either need manual annotations or are limited to rectilinear images. Our approach interpolates depth on spherical grid points by using temporally aggregated point clouds and applies a filtering process to exclude points with high uncertainty or lacking nearby measurements, ensuring minimal error before mapping the remaining points.

rai:dataAnnotationProtocol.evidence: Collected using two 360° cameras in a top-bottom setup and a LiDAR sensor, the dataset includes accurate depth and disparity labels by projecting 3D point clouds onto equirectangular images. Additionally, we provide an augmented training set with an increased label density by using depth completion.

rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis.evidence: To assess alignment accuracy, we calculated the pixel error by measuring Euclidean distances between 200 randomly selected LiDAR points and their image positions, resulting in an average error of 1.7 pixels. When selecting the same number of points from visually challenging areas (e.g., object edges), the error remains relatively low at 8.0 pixels, further confirming calibration quality.

rai:machineAnnotationTools.evidence: Collected using two 360° cameras in a top-bottom setup and a LiDAR sensor, the dataset includes accurate depth and disparity labels by projecting 3D point clouds onto equirectangular images. Additionally, we provide an augmented training set with an increased label density by using depth completion.

rai:personalSensitiveInformation.evidence: To assemble a dataset capturing human pedestrian activity, we built a custom rig and collected data across distinct scenes, encompassing indoor (e.g., corridors, halls) and outdoor (e.g., squares, external parking, footpaths) settings in various lighting conditions on a university campus. The dataset consists of paired top-bottom images with corresponding depth maps, captured from a robot navigating in dynamic human environments.

rai:dataBiases.evidence: While models trained on specific environments perform well within their respective domains, indoor-trained models show a clear limitation in generalizing to outdoor scenes, particularly at night. Furthermore, the data exhibits an exponential decay in pixel percentage with increasing depth, correlating with the decrease in LiDAR precision over longer distances. A distinct concentration of short-range distances within the 0–10 meter range in all settings is attributed to the LiDAR laser capturing the ground surface in each environment.

rai:dataLimitations.evidence: Given this limited temporal window, the error introduced by the movement of the robot, or within the scene, is negligible, given the LiDAR's high frame rate and the rig's sub-pedestrian moving speed. Note that this approach is limited for fast-moving objects like cars. Occlusions were not explicitly handled, as the small LiDAR-camera baseline minimizes their impact. Given the sparse nature of LiDAR point clouds compared to high-resolution camera images, ground-truth depth labels cover only a fraction of the total pixels. It is evident that the depth completion method does not provide labels for pixels at object boundaries.

rai:dataUseCases.evidence: With a total of 39,553 labeled frames, HELVIPAD serves as a foundational resource for developing and benchmarking omnidirectional depth estimation models capable of navigating in human environments. To create the benchmark, we split the captured sequences into a train-val set and a test set, ensuring the same proportion of outdoor, indoor and night outdoor sequences. The train-val set includes 20 sequences – 13 outdoor, 5 indoor and 2 night outdoor sequences – with a total of 29,407 frames. The test split consists of 6 sequences – 3 outdoor, 2 indoor and 1 night outdoor sequences – with a total of 10,146 frames.
